description: JATABELS stands for Journey Ahead Through Ambition, Bravery, Excellence, Leadership, and Strength. In NASA’s Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we embrace lunar exploration by turning space data into insights that help identify promising landing sites through analysis of sunlight and Earth communications. Driven by curiosity, creativity, and fearless innovation, we aim to overcome challenges and contribute to humanity’s next giant leap. JATABELS: Bold ideas, brighter horizons. 🌕🚀
summary:
LULER: Lunar Landing Site Navigator

LULER is an interactive 3D mission planner that helps decide where and when to land on the Moon. Pick any of 25 historical or Artemis-candidate sites, or type any coordinate. LULER then shows, hour by hour for 2027–2028, when the Sun is up for power and when Earth is in view for a direct radio link. Both are tested against the real terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation data, using NAIF SPICE ephemerides checked against JPL Horizons.

Each site gets an explainable 0–100 safety score covering slope, sunlight, Earth contact, night length, and relief. LULER also detects craters, finds the best dates, and compares your point with the two nearest sites. You can fly a Saturn V mission onto real Cesium Moon terrain, ending in a simulated landing that diverts away from hazards. Live NASA DONKI space weather warns of solar radiation storms. An optional AI companion, with free Gemini support and live voice, answers questions from the data and drives the app.

At the lunar south pole, power, communication, and safe ground decide whether a mission survives. LULER makes those trade-offs visible, verifiable, and usable by anyone, using only real NASA data.
details:
LULER – Lunar Landing Site Navigator


Where on the Moon can you land, and when?

What it does


LULER is a free, browser-based mission planner that answers the two questions every lunar landing must solve: where is it safe to land, and when? Users can pick any site on a photorealistic 3D Moon or enter coordinates. LULER then shows, hour by hour across 2027–2028:

  • Whether the site has sunlight for solar power
  • Whether Earth is in view for a direct radio link
  • How steep the ground is
  • Where the craters and hazards are

Each site gets a safety score and a calendar of the best landing days. Users can also fly the full descent, watch the lander automatically divert away from detected craters, and walk the surface in first person.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL SPICE (DE440), computed hourly. We checked them against JPL Horizons, and they agree to within 0.0004°.
  • Terrain comes from NASA LOLA elevation data. Horizon masks use NASA PGDA data on the curved lunar surface, so the mountains and crater rims that really block the Sun and Earth are counted.
  • Crater detection runs a rim-shape test on the elevation grid, and the slope is measured at the exact touchdown point.
  • Live NASA data comes from api.nasa.gov: DONKI space weather (solar flares, particle events, CMEs, geomagnetic storms), EPIC Earth images, and NASA archive photos of each site.
  • The sky uses 6,331 real stars from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue.
  • Every dataset is real. Nothing is invented.

Benefits and impact


LULER turns complex orbital mechanics and terrain analysis into clear, visual decisions. Students, educators, space enthusiasts, and early-stage mission planners can all use it in any browser, for free. It shows why the lunar south pole is so attractive (long sunlight, Earth in view) and why it is so hard (steep slopes, long shadows). This builds public understanding of the Artemis era of exploration.

What makes it creative

  • A Cinematic 3D Moon with a real descent simulation and hazard avoidance
  • A “Here vs on Earth” comparison that makes lunar conditions easy to grasp
  • An AI companion powered by free Google Gemini, with live voice. It can fly users to sites, change dates, and open views on request.
  • 3D team ID cards that showcase Team JATABELS

Tools and technologies


TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, CesiumJS (Cesium Moon Terrain), GSAP, Python, NASA SPICE, LOLA, PGDA, DONKI, EPIC, NASA Image Library, Google Gemini API, GitHub for version control, and Vercel for hosting.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy, validated against JPL Horizons
  • Only real NASA data, with no fake values
  • Works on any device: desktop, tablet, and phone
  • Smooth performance on ordinary laptops
  • A clean interface that non-experts can understand
  • Open-source code anyone can inspect and build on
